concepts.name: Transformers

learning_objectives.name: Trace attention value routing
learning_objectives.description: Trace how queries, keys, attention weights, and values determine which source information reaches each output position.

learning_objectives.name: Predict permutation and order behavior
learning_objectives.description: Predict equivariance, invariance, and order sensitivity when attention has or lacks an explicit positional signal.

learning_objectives.name: Distinguish attention resources from parameters
learning_objectives.description: Predict how sequence length changes pairwise computation and activation memory without confusing those costs with learned parameter count.

learning_objectives.name: Distinguish Transformer information paths
learning_objectives.description: Distinguish which Transformer sublayers mix token positions, preserve residual information, or condition a decoder on encoder outputs.

learning_objectives.name: Diagnose Transformer sublayer composition
learning_objectives.description: Reason about the non-commuting composition of attention, feed-forward, normalization, and residual transformations in a Transformer block.

learning_objectives.name: Apply causal attention visibility
learning_objectives.description: Derive which positions may exchange information under causal, batched, packed, and incremental-decoding attention constraints.

learning_objectives.name: Predict attention logit scaling effects

learning_objectives.name: Trace incremental key-value caching
learning_objectives.description: Trace the tensors retained and recomputed during autoregressive decoding and predict the resulting per-step and total resource costs.

misconceptions.name: Content attention inherently knows absolute position
misconceptions.description: Assumes global token interaction creates order information even when no positional signal is supplied.
misconceptions.remediation: Apply the same permutation to inputs and derive how Q, K, V, and the attention matrix transform.

misconceptions.name: Shared projections destroy permutation equivariance
misconceptions.description: Treats token-shared weight matrices as if they were tied to fixed sequence indices.
misconceptions.remediation: Track tensor shapes: feature projections act identically on every token row.

misconceptions.name: Symmetric pooling recovers order
misconceptions.description: Assumes mean or sum pooling can reconstruct ordering that the representation never encoded.
misconceptions.remediation: Prove that mean and sum are invariant under row permutations.

misconceptions.name: Equivariance means pointwise invariance
misconceptions.description: Confuses an output that follows an input permutation with an output array that remains numerically fixed in place.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the equivariance identity f(PX) = P f(X) and distinguish it from the invariance identity f(PX) = f(X).

misconceptions.name: A token permutation updates only values
misconceptions.description: Permutes the value rows while leaving query-key attention coordinates in their original row and column order.
misconceptions.remediation: Apply the permutation to queries, keys, and values, giving A' = P A P-transpose and V' = P V.

misconceptions.name: Token permutation requires retraining
misconceptions.description: Treats a change in token-row order as a change to the shared learned projection parameters.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the fixed feature-projection weights from the per-example ordering of token activations.

misconceptions.name: Full attention is linear in sequence length
misconceptions.description: Counts token projections but omits the pairwise query-key score matrix.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the L by L attention-score shape before estimating complexity.

misconceptions.name: Transformer parameter count scales with token count
misconceptions.description: Confuses activation sizes for a particular input with learned weights shared across positions.
misconceptions.remediation: List parameter matrices separately from per-example activations.

misconceptions.name: Attention is quadratic only during training
misconceptions.description: Assumes removing backward storage changes the pairwise forward computation into a linear one.
misconceptions.remediation: Distinguish forward asymptotic complexity from the additional constants and storage of backpropagation.

misconceptions.name: Transformers are inherently bidirectional
misconceptions.description: Treats the architecture name as fixing information flow even though attention masks determine which token positions are visible.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the allowed attention edges for causal, bidirectional, and encoder-decoder masks.

misconceptions.name: Position-wise feed-forward layers mix tokens
misconceptions.description: Attributes cross-token communication to the feed-forward sublayer even though its weights are applied independently at each position.
misconceptions.remediation: Track the sequence and feature axes through attention and the position-wise feed-forward network.

misconceptions.name: Residual paths make sublayer order irrelevant
misconceptions.description: Assumes skip connections make attention, normalization, and feed-forward ordering interchangeable.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the computations for two sublayer orders and identify the different inputs seen by each nonlinear transformation.

misconceptions.name: Values determine attention weights
misconceptions.description: Assumes changing value vectors changes the attention distribution even when the query and key vectors are fixed.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the query-key score computation from the later weighted sum of value vectors.

misconceptions.name: Keys are the attention output payloads
misconceptions.description: Treats keys as the vectors summed into an attention output rather than as addresses used to score the associated values.
misconceptions.remediation: Label the roles in softmax(QK-transpose)V and trace which tensor determines weights versus output content.

misconceptions.name: Attention is hard selection
misconceptions.description: Treats softmax attention as an argmax that discards every value except the one with the largest weight.
misconceptions.remediation: Compute a weighted sum with two nonzero attention weights and compare it with an argmax lookup.

misconceptions.name: Residual bypasses erase sublayer updates
misconceptions.description: Assumes the identity path makes a residual block return its input unchanged instead of adding the learned branch output.
misconceptions.remediation: Evaluate x plus the sublayer output explicitly and distinguish preserved input information from an unchanged result.

misconceptions.name: Matching shapes imply commutation
misconceptions.description: Infers that two transformations can be reordered merely because both preserve the representation shape.
misconceptions.remediation: Construct two same-shape nonlinear or affine maps and compare both composition orders on the same input.

misconceptions.name: Layer normalization commutes with residual addition
misconceptions.description: Assumes normalizing a residual sum is equivalent to normalizing only the learned branch and then adding the identity path.
misconceptions.remediation: Compute feature means and variances before and after moving the residual addition across layer normalization.

misconceptions.name: Layer normalization only affects training
misconceptions.description: Treats normalization placement as an optimization-only detail that cannot change a block's forward output at inference.
misconceptions.remediation: Evaluate both normalization placements on a fixed inference-time vector with frozen affine parameters.

misconceptions.name: Layer normalization mixes token positions
misconceptions.description: Attributes cross-token communication to standard per-position layer normalization rather than to attention.
misconceptions.remediation: Mark the axes normalized for one token representation and contrast them with attention's sequence-axis interactions.

misconceptions.name: Decoding caches past queries
misconceptions.description: Assumes future decoding steps need earlier query projections even though each new output forms its own query against retained keys and values.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace one incremental step and label which past tensors are reused by the new query-key scores and value-weighted sum.

misconceptions.name: Multi-query attention shares query heads
misconceptions.description: Interprets multi-query attention as collapsing the query heads rather than sharing key and value projections across them.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the head axes for queries, keys, and values under multi-head and multi-query attention and compare only the changed axes.

misconceptions.name: Key-value sharing collapses time positions
misconceptions.description: Assumes sharing key and value heads removes the need to retain a distinct cached entry for each prior sequence position.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the cache's head axis from its sequence axis and track both as decoding advances.

misconceptions.name: Attention logits are dimension invariant
misconceptions.description: Assumes query-key dot-product variance stays stable as key dimension grows without scaling.
misconceptions.remediation: Compute the variance of a sum of independent coordinate products as key dimension increases.

misconceptions.name: Positive attention scaling reorders keys
misconceptions.description: Claims that dividing every logit by the same positive factor changes their ranking rather than their softmax sharpness.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare rank preservation with the change in exponentiated probability ratios.

misconceptions.name: Unscaled high-dimensional attention becomes uniform
misconceptions.description: Predicts uniform attention when larger dot-product variance instead tends to saturate softmax toward extreme logits.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace how growing logit variance changes softmax entropy and gradients.

misconceptions.name: Causal masks matter only during generation
misconceptions.description: Omits causal masking during teacher-forced training and thereby permits future-token leakage.
misconceptions.remediation: Audit what each training position can attend to when its future target tokens are present in the batch.

misconceptions.name: Causal masking hides the current position
misconceptions.description: Uses a strict-lower-triangular rule where the standard shifted decoder representation may attend through its own position.
misconceptions.remediation: Align input shifting with the j less-than-or-equal-to i attention rule for each prediction position.

misconceptions.name: Causal dependence forces serial training
misconceptions.description: Confuses a dependency restriction in attention with a requirement to compute teacher-forced training positions one at a time.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate parallel masked matrix operations in training from sequential token availability during generation.

misconceptions.name: Target causal masking truncates encoder memory
misconceptions.description: Applies the decoder target-index causal triangle to encoder cross-attention and hides later source positions even when the complete source is available.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the future-target boundary in decoder self-attention from cross-attention over the fully encoded nonpadding source.

questions.stem: A self-attention layer uses shared query, key, and value projections but no positional encodings or position-dependent mask. If the input token rows are permuted, what happens to the token outputs and to a classifier that mean-pools those outputs?

options.text: Token outputs remain in their original order because global attention reconstructs absolute positions from pairwise scores.
options.rationale: Pairwise content scores contain no absolute index signal; global access alone does not break permutation symmetry.

options.text: Token outputs change arbitrarily because the learned projection matrices are tied to fixed row indices.
options.rationale: The projections are shared across rows, so permuting input rows simply permutes Q, K, V, and the corresponding outputs.

options.text: Token outputs are permuted in the same way, and mean pooling produces the same classifier input as before.
options.rationale: Unpositioned self-attention is permutation equivariant, and mean pooling converts that equivariance into permutation invariance.

options.text: Token outputs are equivariant, but mean pooling recovers the original sequence order and therefore changes the classifier input.
options.rationale: Mean pooling is symmetric and cannot recover or react to row order.

questions.stem: A standard full self-attention block keeps hidden width, head count, batch size, and weights fixed while sequence length increases from L to 2L. Ignoring implementation-specific kernels, which scaling statement is most accurate?

options.text: Parameters and attention work both roughly double, because each additional token is processed once.
options.rationale: Token projections are linear in L, but the full query-key and attention-value interactions involve L squared pairs.

options.text: Parameters and attention work both roughly quadruple, because the model learns one weight set per token pair.
options.rationale: Pairwise activations grow quadratically, but projection and feed-forward weights are shared across positions and do not grow with input length.

options.text: Training attention roughly quadruples, but inference attention merely doubles because no gradient tensors are stored.
options.rationale: Backward storage affects constants and memory, not the L squared pairwise computation required by the full forward pass.

options.text: Parameters stay fixed; pairwise attention terms grow about fourfold, while token-wise projection work grows about twofold.
options.rationale: Weights are length independent, L-by-L terms scale quadratically, and per-token operations scale linearly.

questions.stem: The same Transformer block is used once with unrestricted self-attention and once with a causal mask that blocks positions to the right. What architectural property changes most directly?

options.text: The causal version gains bidirectional context because Transformer layers impose two-way information flow by design.
options.rationale: The causal mask removes rightward attention edges, so information flow is not inherently bidirectional.

options.text: The position-wise feed-forward network begins mixing neighboring tokens because masking shifts communication out of attention.
options.rationale: The feed-forward sublayer remains independently applied at each token position.

options.text: Residual paths erase the difference because skipped representations make the attention mask operationally irrelevant.
options.rationale: A residual adds the input to a mask-dependent attention output; it does not restore blocked future information.

options.text: The allowed token-to-token information paths change, enabling full-context encoding in one case and autoregressive conditioning in the other.
options.rationale: Attention masks define which positions can contribute to each representation while leaving the core block parameters reusable.

questions.stem: In a standard Transformer layer, attention output is temporarily replaced with zeros while the position-wise feed-forward sublayer and residual paths remain. Which operation can still combine information from different token positions in that layer?

options.text: No remaining operation; each token is transformed separately from its own residual representation in this layer.
options.rationale: Cross-token mixing is supplied by attention, while the feed-forward network acts separately along the feature axis at each position.

options.text: The feed-forward sublayer, because its two learned matrices multiply across the sequence axis and exchange token content.
options.rationale: Those matrices are shared across positions but applied independently to each position's feature vector.

options.text: The residual path, because adding a token representation incorporates representations from neighboring sequence locations.
options.rationale: A residual addition combines two representations at the same position; it does not itself connect positions.

options.text: Bidirectional Transformer structure, because token communication persists without attention or another sequence-mixing operation.
options.rationale: The architecture label does not create information paths after the sequence-mixing operation is removed.

questions.stem: A developer swaps the attention and position-wise feed-forward sublayers in a trained Transformer block without changing their parameters. Residual connections are retained. Why should identical outputs not be expected?

options.text: The swap forces attention to become unidirectional because later sublayers determine whether a Transformer is bidirectional.
options.rationale: Directionality is controlled by permitted attention edges, not merely by whether attention appears before the feed-forward map.

options.text: The nonlinear sublayers receive different inputs and generally do not commute, so residual additions do not make their order equivalent.
options.rationale: Composing nonlinear attention and feed-forward transformations in opposite orders changes the intermediate representation each sees.

options.text: The swap makes the feed-forward matrices mix token positions, changing which sequence elements exchange their feature vectors.
options.rationale: Position-wise feed-forward maps do not acquire cross-token mixing when moved earlier in the block.

options.text: The outputs should match because residual paths make the ordering of attention and feed-forward transformations irrelevant.
options.rationale: Residual connections preserve an identity path but do not make the added nonlinear transformations commutative.

questions.stem: In one attention head, a query assigns weights 0.8 and 0.2 to two source positions whose value vectors are v1 and v2. Ignoring output projection, what does the head return for that query?

options.text: The value from the absolute query position, because content attention recovers sequence coordinates without positional input.
options.rationale: The stated computation routes source values by compatibility weights and supplies no absolute position by itself.

options.text: The weighted mixture 0.8 v1 + 0.2 v2, so query-key compatibility controls how source values are aggregated.
options.rationale: After softmax, attention weights form the coefficients of the value-vector combination for that query.

options.text: A row-specific projection of v1, because shared query and key matrices bind learned parameters to token indices.
options.rationale: Shared projections act on token content uniformly; the weights arise from content compatibility.

options.text: A linear-time summary independent of source count, because full attention avoids pairwise query-key interactions.
options.rationale: This two-source mixture is simple, but forming all query-key scores in full attention is pairwise in sequence length.

questions.stem: A self-attention layer has shared query, key, and value projections and no positional signal. If its input tokens are permuted, which joint prediction about token outputs and score computation is correct?

options.text: The token outputs permute with the inputs, while full attention still forms a pairwise score matrix.
options.rationale: Without positional information the shared layer is permutation equivariant, and full query-key interaction still evaluates token pairs.

options.text: The pairwise scores let the layer reconstruct each token's original absolute position before producing its outputs.
options.rationale: Content similarities do not identify an absolute index that was never supplied to the layer.

options.text: Shared projections bind semantic roles to fixed array slots, so the outputs remain in their original positions.
options.rationale: Applying the same projections at every position preserves, rather than destroys, the corresponding permutation of outputs.

options.text: The token outputs permute with the inputs, and projection sharing makes the full score computation linear in token count.
options.rationale: Shared parameters do not remove the quadratic number of query-key pairs in unrestricted full attention.

questions.stem: A positionless full self-attention layer with fixed hidden width is run first on 100 tokens and then on 200 tokens. Which prediction correctly combines learned parameters, pairwise scores, and permutation behavior?

options.text: Score entries quadruple, and those scores reveal each token's original absolute index without added position features.
options.rationale: The matrix grows quadratically, but content-based scores do not create absent absolute-position information.

options.text: Projection parameters stay fixed, score entries quadruple, and permuting tokens correspondingly permutes their outputs.
options.rationale: Weights are shared across positions, whereas an unrestricted score matrix grows from 100 squared to 200 squared entries.

options.text: Projection parameters double because shared weights attach to slots, and a token permutation no longer produces a matching output permutation.
options.rationale: Token-shared matrices neither duplicate with sequence length nor attach their computation to a fixed slot identity.

options.text: Projection parameters stay fixed and outputs permute, but the number of full-attention score entries merely doubles.
options.rationale: Doubling both score-matrix dimensions multiplies the number of pairwise entries by four.

questions.stem: Query and key coordinates are roughly independent, zero mean, and unit variance. As key dimension grows, why does scaled dot-product attention divide their dot product by the square root of that dimension?

options.text: It changes the key ranking so softmax can choose a different maximum even when all logits receive the same divisor.
options.rationale: A shared positive divisor preserves logit order, although it changes probability ratios.

options.text: It is unnecessary because dot-product variance stays fixed as coordinates are added, leaving softmax behavior dimension invariant.
options.rationale: Under the stated assumptions, summing additional coordinate products increases the logit variance.

options.text: It counteracts a tendency for high-dimensional unscaled dot products to converge toward equal logits and uniform attention weights.
options.rationale: The variance grows rather than collapses, so unscaled logits tend toward extreme softmax behavior, not equality.

options.text: It normalizes the growing dot-product variance, reducing softmax saturation while preserving the ordering of keys for that query.
options.rationale: Dividing by the standard-deviation scale stabilizes logit magnitude without changing their rank.

questions.stem: A transformer doubles its query-key dimension but removes the square-root scaling, while coordinate statistics remain similar. What failure mode is most plausible early in training?

options.text: Larger-magnitude logits can make softmax overly sharp and gradients poorly conditioned because their variance was not normalized.
options.rationale: Summing more coordinate products increases logit variance, which can push softmax into saturated regions.

options.text: The attention distribution becomes nearly uniform because additional coordinate products force all query-key scores toward the same value.
options.rationale: Additional terms increase score variance; they do not make distinct dot products converge to one value.

options.text: The attention distribution is statistically unchanged because raw dot-product scale does not depend on the number of key coordinates.
options.rationale: Under the stated assumptions, the variance of the summed products grows with dimension.

options.text: Key preference reverses because omitting a shared positive divisor changes which query-key dot product has the largest rank.
options.rationale: A positive common scaling changes softmax sharpness, not the ordering of the logits.

questions.stem: For one query, attention logits are [8, 4, 0]. They are divided by a positive temperature-like scale before softmax. Which property is preserved and which property changes?

options.text: The variance is dimension invariant, so neither logit magnitude nor the softmax probabilities depend on the chosen scale.
options.rationale: Softmax probability ratios depend directly on scaled logit differences.

options.text: The key ranking is preserved, while the probability gaps and entropy change because softmax responds to logit scale.
options.rationale: Positive common scaling is order preserving, but it changes exponentiated ratios among the logits.

options.text: The highest and lowest keys can exchange rank, while softmax entropy stays fixed because all logits share the divisor.
options.rationale: The ranking cannot reverse under a shared positive divisor, and softmax entropy generally changes.

options.text: The probabilities move toward equality as dimension grows because unscaled high-dimensional attention naturally produces uniform scores.
options.rationale: Dimension growth raises unscaled variance under the usual assumptions; the explicit scale controls sharpness.

questions.stem: During teacher-forced decoder training, every target token is present in the batch. What does the causal attention mask prevent at the representation used to predict position i?

options.text: It removes the current position as well as future positions, since a causal representation may use tokens strictly before i.
options.rationale: With the standard shifted decoder inputs, attention can include the current input position while blocking later ones.

options.text: It is inactive in training and blocks future positions after generation begins, when target tokens are no longer batched.
options.rationale: Without the training mask, a position could leak information from future targets already present in the batch.

options.text: It blocks attention from position i to positions after i, so the prediction does not use future-token information available during training.
options.rationale: The mask enforces the autoregressive information boundary even though all teacher-forced positions are computed together.

options.text: It forces the training loop to run one token at a time, since masked dependencies are not representable by parallel matrix operations.
options.rationale: A triangular mask is applied in parallel to the attention-logit matrix during training.

questions.stem: A shifted decoder input has positions indexed from 0 through n-1. Which attention rule gives the standard causal self-attention visibility for query position i?

options.text: Permit all j during training, then apply j less than or equal to i when decoding generated tokens.
options.rationale: Training needs the same future-information boundary because future target positions coexist in the input tensor.

options.text: Permit j greater than i, since the shifted target representation should flow backward from future tokens.
options.rationale: This exposes future positions and reverses the autoregressive dependency rather than enabling safe parallelism.

options.text: Permit j strictly less than i, since including the current shifted input position leaks the target being predicted.
options.rationale: Input shifting separates the current input token from its next-token target, so the diagonal can remain visible.

options.text: Permit j less than or equal to i and mask j greater than i, while computing all permitted rows in parallel.
options.rationale: The lower-triangular visibility rule blocks future positions without serializing the masked training computation.

questions.stem: An engineer claims causal language-model training must call the decoder once per token because each prediction depends on its prefix. Which correction is most precise?

options.text: Teacher forcing supplies the shifted sequence, so all positions can be computed in parallel under a mask that blocks future keys.
options.rationale: The dependency is enforced by triangular visibility in a parallel attention matrix; generation remains sequential in token availability.

options.text: The claim is correct because causal masking turns each attention matrix operation into a serial recurrence over positions.
options.rationale: Masking zeros disallowed logits but does not require serial evaluation of teacher-forced rows.

options.text: Training can be parallel by removing the mask; causal visibility is needed later during generation but not for fitted targets.
options.rationale: Removing the mask during training would let positions exploit future target information.

options.text: Training can be parallel if each position also hides its diagonal entry, which removes any use of the current shifted input token.
options.rationale: Parallelism does not depend on hiding the diagonal, and standard shifted decoder attention can include it.

questions.stem: The same trained Transformer checkpoint processes sequences of 64 and 128 tokens. Activation memory grows, but the stored parameter tensors are unchanged. Which account is correct?

options.text: Doubling the tokens silently created another copy of each learned matrix, so parameter count grew with activation memory.
options.rationale: The learned projections are shared across positions; per-example activations grow without duplicating the stored weights.

options.text: Shared parameter matrices were applied at more positions, changing activation shapes while leaving the checkpoint parameter count fixed.
options.rationale: Sequence length changes the number of position activations and attention interactions, not the number of shared learned matrices.

options.text: The longer sequence became bidirectional by construction, which explains the extra memory without reference to its attention mask.
options.rationale: Information direction is set by allowed attention edges; it is not determined by input length or the Transformer label.

options.text: The position-wise feed-forward sublayer allocated new cross-token weights so it could exchange information among the added positions.
options.rationale: The feed-forward map is shared and applied independently at each position; attention supplies cross-position mixing.

questions.stem: For one query with key dimension 64, the unscaled dot products for three keys are 16, 8, and 0. What does standard square-root scaling do before softmax?

options.text: It divides each logit by a different key-dependent value, so the three keys can change their ranking.
options.rationale: Standard scaled dot-product attention uses the same positive divisor for each logit associated with this query.

options.text: It leaves the logits at 16, 8, and 0 because their variance does not depend on the key dimension.
options.rationale: The square-root factor addresses dimension-dependent dot-product magnitude and is not an identity operation here.

options.text: It produces logits 2, 1, and 0, preserving their order while making the resulting softmax less saturated.
options.rationale: The divisor is the square root of 64, which is 8; common positive scaling preserves rank while changing probability ratios.

options.text: It produces equal logits because scaling high-dimensional dot products is intended to force a uniform attention distribution.
options.rationale: Scaling stabilizes magnitude but does not erase the differences among the original dot products.

questions.stem: A decoder is teacher-forced on a four-token sequence in one batched matrix operation. Which visibility rule prevents target leakage while retaining parallel training?

options.text: Use unrestricted attention during training and add the causal mask later during generation, when leakage can first occur.
options.rationale: Future target tokens are present during teacher forcing, so unrestricted training attention would leak them into earlier predictions.

options.text: Permit positions strictly before each row and hide its aligned current input position as part of the causal rule.
options.rationale: With the standard shifted decoder input, a row may attend through its aligned position while future positions remain blocked.

options.text: Evaluate one row at a time because causal dependence makes a batched masked attention matrix mathematically invalid.
options.rationale: Teacher forcing supplies all shifted inputs, allowing the masked attention rows to be computed in parallel.

options.text: Allow row i to attend through column i and earlier columns, block later columns, and compute all masked rows together.
options.rationale: A lower-triangular inclusive mask enforces prefix visibility while preserving parallel matrix computation during training.

questions.stem: An engineer removes self-attention from a Transformer block but keeps a position-wise feed-forward network and residual paths. The replacement has a similar parameter count. What capability changed?

options.text: Cross-token reasoning remains because learned parameter count, which scales with token count, stayed approximately constant.
options.rationale: Parameter count and token interaction are different properties, and shared learned weights do not scale with sequence length.

options.text: Cross-token reasoning moves into the position-wise feed-forward matrices, which exchange features among sequence locations.
options.rationale: Those matrices transform each position independently and do not create sequence-axis communication.

options.text: The block loses its sequence-mixing operation; a comparable parameter count does not replace attention's token-to-token paths.
options.rationale: Attention supplies cross-position communication, while residual and position-wise maps operate on information already present at each position.

options.text: Cross-token reasoning is unchanged because residual connections make the presence and ordering of nonlinear sublayers irrelevant.
options.rationale: Residual paths preserve an identity contribution but do not recreate a removed sequence-mixing transformation.

questions.stem: Two attention heads receive identical raw query-key dot products. One implementation mistakenly divides by the square root of key dimension twice instead of once. What changes?

options.text: The extra positive divisor can reverse the key ranking, so a different key becomes the largest logit.
options.rationale: Applying another shared positive divisor preserves the ordering of all logits for that query.

options.text: Nothing changes because dot-product magnitude is dimension invariant and the scaling factors cancel in softmax.
options.rationale: Softmax is sensitive to common positive scaling, and the dimension factor does not cancel from its probability ratios.

options.text: The extra division prevents the uniform distribution that unscaled high-dimensional attention would otherwise approach.
options.rationale: Unscaled variance tends to make softmax sharper, while excessive division can flatten it toward uniformity.

options.text: The key ranking stays fixed, but the twice-scaled logits produce a flatter softmax than the correctly scaled head.
options.rationale: Additional common positive scaling reduces logit gaps without changing their order, increasing attention entropy.

questions.stem: A Transformer uses unrestricted self-attention but receives no positional encoding or other position signal. Two inputs contain the same token representations in different orders. What behavior should an audit expect?

options.text: The outputs can follow the same permutation because shared attention and feed-forward operations lack a signal that identifies absolute order.
options.rationale: Without position information, permuting input positions correspondingly permutes the outputs of the shared sequence operations.

options.text: The unrestricted Transformer recovers the original order because bidirectional attention carries an intrinsic left-to-right coordinate system.
options.rationale: Unrestricted visibility says which positions may interact but does not attach an intrinsic order label to them.

options.text: The position-wise feed-forward sublayer reconstructs the order by mixing neighboring token locations after each attention operation.
options.rationale: That sublayer applies the same feature transformation independently at each position and supplies no sequence-axis order signal.

options.text: The reordered input creates a different set of learned matrices because Transformer parameter count varies with token placement.
options.rationale: The parameter matrices are shared across positions and remain unchanged when token order or sequence length changes.

questions.stem: In an encoder-decoder Transformer, the decoder's cross-attention sublayer is removed while masked self-attention, feed-forward layers, and residual paths remain. What information path is lost?

options.text: No information path is lost because residual connections make the removed nonlinear sublayer operationally interchangeable with the others.
options.rationale: A residual preserves the decoder-side input but does not recreate access to encoder representations.

options.text: The decoder loses its direct route to encoder representations; its remaining sublayers process decoder-side state without that source context.
options.rationale: Cross-attention supplies keys and values from the encoder, so removing it severs the modeled source-to-decoder connection.

options.text: The feed-forward layer inherits the encoder sequence and mixes its positions because cross-token communication shifts into its matrices.
options.rationale: The position-wise feed-forward layer has no encoder input and does not mix sequence positions.

options.text: Masked self-attention becomes bidirectional and therefore obtains the missing encoder information through the architecture's directionality.
options.rationale: Decoder self-attention uses decoder states under its mask and cannot access an encoder tensor that is no longer connected.

questions.stem: A classifier must assign different labels to token sequences A-B and B-A. It uses positionless self-attention followed by mean pooling. Why can this architecture not learn the required distinction from token order alone?

options.text: Self-attention already infers absolute positions from global interaction, so the failure comes from insufficient training data.
options.rationale: Global content interaction does not supply an absolute or relative position signal when none is encoded.

options.text: Shared query, key, and value projections attach different learned matrices to A-B and B-A, destroying permutation equivariance.
options.rationale: Shared projections apply the same feature maps to token rows and preserve the corresponding permutation structure.

options.text: Attention outputs permute with the input, and mean pooling removes that permutation, yielding the same pooled representation.
options.rationale: Positionless attention is permutation equivariant and symmetric pooling is invariant, so their composition cannot encode this order label.

options.text: Mean pooling reconstructs the missing order from the set of output vectors, so the architecture should separate both sequences.
options.rationale: Mean pooling is unchanged by row permutation and cannot recover order that the representation did not encode.

questions.stem: A positionless attention head has A = [[0.75, 0.25], [0.20, 0.80]], V = [4, 0] transpose, and Y = AV = [3.0, 0.8] transpose. The two token rows are swapped. Shared projections imply A' = P A P-transpose and V' = P V. What is Y' = A'V'?

options.text: Y' = [3.0, 0.8] transpose; equivariance means the numeric output array stays fixed in place.
options.rationale: Equivariance means the output follows the input permutation, not that each array position retains its old value.

options.text: Y' = [0.8, 3.0] transpose; the output rows follow the same swap applied to the token rows.
options.rationale: A'V' = (P A P-transpose)(P V) = P A V = P Y, which swaps the two original output rows.

options.text: Y' = [1.0, 3.2] transpose; V is permuted while A stays in its original coordinates.
options.rationale: That vector equals A(PV), but the query-key score rows and columns must be permuted along with the values.

options.text: Y' is undetermined until the shared projections are retrained for the swapped token-row order.
options.rationale: The projection parameters are shared across token rows and do not change when an input example is reordered.

questions.stem: For one attention head, the 64 coordinate products q_r k_r are independent, zero mean, and each has variance 9. What is the variance of the scaled logit (q dot k) / sqrt(64), and what does it demonstrate?

options.text: It is 9/64; the unscaled dot product retains variance 9 as dimension grows, and square-root division then reduces that variance by 64.
options.rationale: Independent coordinate-product variances add, so the raw variance is 64 times 9 rather than 9.

options.text: It approaches 0, because adding independent high-dimensional terms drives the attention scores toward equality and uniform weights.
options.rationale: Independent variances add; increasing key dimension expands raw score variance rather than collapsing every score to the same value.

options.text: It is 9; square-root scaling removes the factor from summing 64 terms but does not remove their non-unit coordinate scale.
options.rationale: The raw variance is 64 times 9, and division by sqrt(64) divides variance by 64, leaving 9.

options.text: It is 9, but the scaling can change which key has the largest logit because each key's ranking depends on the divisor.
options.rationale: The numeric variance is right, but one shared positive divisor preserves the ordering of keys for a fixed query.

questions.stem: A trained attention head has zero-mean query-key coordinate products, but products from different coordinates are strongly correlated. An audit claims division by sqrt(d_k) therefore guarantees unit-variance logits. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: The guarantee holds because raw dot-product variance is dimension invariant even when coordinate products are correlated.
options.rationale: Covariance terms contribute to the variance of the sum, so neither the raw variance nor its scaled value is universally fixed.

options.text: The guarantee is unnecessary because correlation makes high-dimensional logits converge to equality and yields uniform attention.
options.rationale: Correlation need not collapse logits or force uniform weights; it can instead increase or decrease their variance.

options.text: The guarantee fails because the common positive divisor can reorder keys once cross-coordinate covariance is present.
options.rationale: For a fixed query, dividing every finite logit by the same positive scalar preserves their ordering regardless of covariance.

options.text: The guarantee is too strong: sqrt(d_k) controls nominal growth under approximate independence, while covariance terms can alter the resulting variance.
options.rationale: The standard variance argument assumes roughly independent unit-scale coordinate products; learned correlations add covariance terms not canceled by sqrt(d_k).

questions.stem: Two unrelated training examples are concatenated into one packed decoder row, with the second example placed after the first. A single global lower-triangular attention mask is applied. What additional constraint is needed for independent-example semantics?

options.text: Remove masking during packed training and restore it during generation, when cross-example leakage can first affect predictions.
options.rationale: All packed target tokens are available during teacher forcing, so training requires causal visibility and example-boundary isolation.

options.text: Use a strict lower triangle within the whole packed row, hiding each position's aligned shifted input as well as later positions.
options.rationale: A strict diagonal does not isolate the examples and incorrectly removes the standard aligned shifted-input position.

options.text: Run every token of each example serially, because segment boundaries make a parallel masked attention matrix invalid.
options.rationale: A block-diagonal causal mask can represent both within-example prefix visibility and segment isolation in one parallel operation.

options.text: Combine the causal rule with a segment-boundary mask so tokens cannot attend to positions belonging to the other example.
options.rationale: A global lower triangle blocks future positions but still exposes the earlier packed example; segment-aware blocks remove that unintended path.

questions.stem: During incremental decoder inference, one new query is evaluated against a key-value cache containing only its permitted prefix and its current input position; no future keys exist. Is a full triangular mask required for this attention call?

options.text: Yes; causal masking is reserved for inference, so every generation call needs a materialized triangular matrix despite absent future keys.
options.rationale: Causality is also enforced during training, and in this single-query call the cache contents already restrict the visible key set.

options.text: No; for this single query, only permitted positions exist in the cache, although batching unequal positions may still require masking.
options.rationale: When the key set contains no future position, attending over the entire cache is causal; padding or multi-position batching can add separate mask requirements.

options.text: Yes; the mask must hide the current cached key as well as nonexistent future keys, leaving access strictly to earlier positions.
options.rationale: With the standard shifted decoder alignment, the current input position is permitted; causality blocks positions to its right.

options.text: No; but the query must be recomputed once per cached key because causal dependence prevents a vectorized attention operation.
options.rationale: The single query can score every permitted cached key in one vectorized operation; masking and serial matrix evaluation are separate issues.

questions.stem: A decoder generates L tokens autoregressively. Without a key-value cache, it recomputes full-prefix self-attention at every step; with an exact cache, each step projects only the new token and attends from its new query to all cached keys. For fixed width and layer count, which asymptotic comparison is correct?

options.text: Cached decoding is O(L) in total attention scores because producing one token per step makes full attention linear in sequence length.
options.rationale: The new query scores a growing prefix, so summing 1 through L cached-key comparisons is quadratic, not linear.

options.text: The cache turns prior keys and values into learned parameters, so parameter count grows with L even though computation falls.
options.rationale: Cached keys and values are input-dependent activations; the learned projection matrices remain shared and fixed in size.

options.text: Naive recomputation sums O(t squared) attention work over prefixes, giving O(L cubed), while caching sums O(t) new-query scores, giving O(L squared).
options.rationale: Recomputing every prefix score matrix costs the sum of t squared, whereas exact caching retains past projections and forms one growing score row per step.

options.text: Both versions are O(L) at inference because quadratic attention is a training artifact of retaining gradient tensors.
options.rationale: Removing backpropagation does not remove pairwise forward score computations; caching changes their reuse pattern but leaves quadratic total scoring.

questions.stem: An encoder-decoder Transformer has S source positions and T decoder positions. In the decoder cross-attention sublayer, which assignment produces a T-by-S compatibility matrix and source-conditioned decoder outputs?

options.text: Project T decoder states as queries and S encoder states as keys and values, then compute decoder-query by encoder-key scores.
options.rationale: Each decoder position queries the encoded source; Q_dec K_enc-transpose has shape T by S and weights encoder-derived values.

options.text: Use encoder states for queries, keys, and values because Transformer cross-attention is inherently bidirectional and needs no decoder-side query.
options.rationale: Cross-attention direction follows the assigned tensors; the decoder state supplies each output position's query into the encoder memory.

options.text: Let the position-wise feed-forward matrices multiply the T and S axes, while attention independently transforms each decoder position.
options.rationale: The feed-forward sublayer acts separately at each decoder position; cross-attention creates the T-by-S sequence interaction.

options.text: Allocate learned projection matrices with T-by-S dimensions, so changing source or target length creates a different parameter set.
options.rationale: Projection weights act on feature dimensions and are shared across positions; T and S affect activation shapes, not learned parameter count.

questions.stem: An attention head has fixed query and key projections, giving weights [0.7, 0.2, 0.1] for one query. Before the output projection, an engineer replaces only the second source value v2 with v2-prime. What follows?

options.text: The weights stay [0.7, 0.2, 0.1], while the pre-projection output becomes 0.7v1 + 0.2v2-prime + 0.1v3.
options.rationale: Queries and keys determine the softmax weights; those fixed weights then combine the possibly changed value vectors.

options.text: The weights must change because each value vector participates in the query-key compatibility score used by softmax.
options.rationale: Scaled dot-product attention computes its weights from queries and keys, not from the value vectors that are subsequently combined.

options.text: Neither the weights nor the output can change because the output is the weighted sum of the fixed key vectors.
options.rationale: Keys participate in addressing; the softmax weights multiply values to form the head output.

options.text: Only v1 can affect the output because attention returns the value at the largest-weight position and discards the rest.
options.rationale: Ordinary softmax attention is a weighted sum, so every source with nonzero weight contributes.

questions.stem: For a one-dimensional audit, ignore normalization and wrap each sublayer S as R_S(z) = z + S(z). Let the attention map be A(z) = 2z and the feed-forward map be F(z) = z + 1. Starting from z = 1, what are R_F(R_A(z)) and R_A(R_F(z))?

options.text: They are both 5 because residual paths make the two sublayer orders equivalent to adding A(z) and F(z) at the original z.
options.rationale: Sequential residual composition changes the input to the second map, so the paths do not make the transformations order-independent.

options.text: They are 7 and 9, respectively; the second residual sublayer receives the first sublayer's updated representation.
options.rationale: R_A(1) is 3 and R_F(3) is 7, whereas R_F(1) is 3 and R_A(3) is 9.

options.text: They are both 1 because an identity residual bypass preserves the original value and erases each learned branch's update.
options.rationale: A residual connection adds the identity value to the branch output; it does not replace the sum with the identity alone.

options.text: They are both 7 because residual maps with the same input and output shape necessarily commute.
options.rationale: Shape compatibility permits either composition but does not make the functions commute; the reverse order evaluates to 9.

questions.stem: A block from the original post-normalization Transformer computes y = LayerNorm(x + S(x)). A refactor instead computes y-prime = x + LayerNorm(S(x)), using the same frozen sublayer and normalization parameters. Which review is correct?

options.text: The refactor is generally equivalent because layer normalization commutes with adding the residual branch.
options.rationale: Layer normalization uses statistics of its input, so normalizing x + S(x) is not generally the same as adding x after normalizing S(x).

options.text: The two expressions differ during optimization but become identical at inference once all parameters are frozen.
options.rationale: Layer normalization is part of the deterministic forward computation at inference, so moving it changes the evaluated function.

options.text: The refactor can change inference outputs because it changes the normalized vector and puts the identity path outside normalization.
options.rationale: The two expressions are different functions under fixed parameters; no training-time randomness is required for them to differ.

options.text: The relevant difference is that the refactor lets layer normalization mix information between token positions before adding x.
options.rationale: Standard Transformer layer normalization acts within each position's feature vector; moving it does not create cross-token communication.

questions.stem: At one decoder layer, ordinary multi-head attention has h query heads and separately caches keys and values for h heads. It is replaced by multi-query attention with the same h query heads but one shared key head and one shared value head. For the same generated length and per-head width, which cache account is correct?

options.text: The cache still needs h histories for queries, keys, and values because later steps reuse every earlier query projection.
options.rationale: A new step forms a new query; its reusable prefix state consists of prior keys and values, not prior queries.

options.text: The factor-h reduction comes from keeping only one time position, because shared keys and values collapse the entire prefix into one cache entry.
options.rationale: The shared dimension is the head axis; distinct earlier sequence positions remain available to the new query.

options.text: The cache can shrink only if the h query heads are also replaced by one query head, because multi-query attention shares queries rather than keys and values.
options.rationale: Multi-query attention retains multiple query heads while sharing the key and value heads used by them.

options.text: The key-value cache's head-axis size falls by a factor of h, while it still retains one key and value entry for every prior position and preserves h query heads.
options.rationale: Multi-query attention shares one key-value pair of heads across the h query heads; sharing heads does not remove the sequence history.

questions.stem: A unit test evaluates a positionless self-attention function H on token matrix X and on PX, where P swaps token rows. The projections are shared across rows and there is no position-dependent mask. Which assertion is the correct equivariance contract?

options.text: Assert H(PX) = H(X), because equivariance requires each numeric output row to remain fixed after the input rows move.
options.rationale: Equivariance moves the output rows with the input permutation; an unchanged output array would be pointwise invariance.

options.text: Permute the value rows inside H but leave the query-key score rows and columns at their original token indices.
options.rationale: Permuting tokens changes the query and key rows too, so the attention matrix coordinates must move along with the values.

options.text: Assert H(PX) = P H(X), because the attention coordinates and value rows transform together under the same row permutation.
options.rationale: With shared row-wise projections and no positional mechanism, self-attention is permutation equivariant: the output follows the input row permutation.

options.text: Defer the assertion until H is retrained on row-swapped examples, because the shared projections acquire a different parameterization for PX.
options.rationale: A row permutation changes the input arrangement, not the shared projection parameters, so the relation is testable without retraining.

questions.stem: For a fixed input, an attention head keeps its query and key projection matrices unchanged but replaces its value projection matrix. Ignore the output projection. Which internal trace is generally correct?

options.text: Both the probability matrix and output must change because the projected values participate in the compatibility logits.
options.rationale: The compatibility logits use queries and keys; replacing the value projection does not enter that calculation.

options.text: Neither quantity changes because the fixed keys are the payload vectors that the probability matrix combines into the output.
options.rationale: Keys determine addressing scores, while the possibly changed projected values supply the vectors being combined.

options.text: The probabilities stay fixed, and the output can change only if the identity of the largest-weight source position changes.
options.rationale: Softmax attention combines every nonzero-weight value, so changed values can alter the output without changing the largest-weight position.

options.text: The probability matrix stays fixed because queries and keys are fixed, while the weighted output generally changes with the projected values.
options.rationale: Scaled dot-product attention first forms softmax weights from queries and keys and then multiplies those weights by the value matrix.

questions.stem: A multi-query decoder layer has eight query heads, one shared key head, one shared value head, and head width d. Before processing the next token, t prior positions are cached. Using [sequence, heads, width] and omitting batch and layer axes, which tensor inventory is correct?

options.text: Cache past Q, K, and V as [t, 8, d], since future steps reuse the complete projections from prior heads.
options.rationale: Future steps reuse prior keys and values; each step creates its own current queries rather than attending with cached past queries.

options.text: Cache K and V as [1, 1, d], since sharing their head axis also summarizes all t prior positions into one entry.
options.rationale: Head sharing does not collapse the sequence axis; the cache retains a key and value for every prior position.

options.text: Cache K and V as [t, 1, d], and form the current transient Q as [1, 8, d] for the next attention call.
options.rationale: Multi-query attention preserves the query-head axis but shares one key-value head across those queries while retaining all prefix positions.

options.text: Cache K and V as [t, 8, d] but form Q as [1, 1, d], because multi-query attention shares the queries rather than the keys and values.
options.rationale: The defining sharing is one key head and one value head across multiple query heads, not one query head across multiple key-value heads.

questions.stem: A sequential residual block computes h = x + A(x), then y = h + F(h). An optimizer proposes y-prime = x + A(x) + F(x), evaluating both branches from x in parallel. Which review criterion directly tests the claimed equivalence?

options.text: No functional test is needed because residual paths make sequential and parallel sublayer orderings equivalent by construction.
options.rationale: The identity additions do not remove the dependence of F on the intermediate h produced by the first sublayer.

options.text: Check that y equals x, because the identity bypass erases A and F whenever residual connections are present.
options.rationale: A residual path preserves x by addition while retaining, rather than erasing, the branch transformations.

options.text: Check that A and F preserve the same tensor shape, which is sufficient to establish that their residual compositions commute.
options.rationale: Matching domains and codomains make both expressions well formed but do not establish equality or commutation.

options.text: Find an x for which F(x + A(x)) differs from F(x); such a case demonstrates that the parallel rewrite changes y.
options.rationale: The sequential expression contains F(x + A(x)), whereas the proposed expression contains F(x); a differing evaluation is a direct counterexample.

questions.stem: For one token with two features, let x = [1, 0] and S(x) = [0, 2]. LayerNorm has unit scale and zero bias; ignore epsilon. What do y = LayerNorm(x + S(x)) and y-prime = x + LayerNorm(S(x)) evaluate to?

options.text: Both are [-1, 1], because layer normalization commutes with moving the residual addition across it.
options.rationale: The first normalization sees [1, 2], while the second sees [0, 2] before x is added, so the expressions are not interchangeable.

options.text: Both are [1, 0], because frozen layer normalization affects optimization but is inactive during this forward calculation.
options.rationale: Layer normalization remains an active deterministic transformation when its learned scale and bias are frozen.

options.text: They are [-1, 1] and [0, 1], respectively; normalization uses different feature vectors in the two expressions.
options.rationale: Normalizing [1, 2] yields [-1, 1]; normalizing [0, 2] yields [-1, 1], and then adding x gives [0, 1].

options.text: The result is underdetermined without the other token positions, because layer normalization computes its statistics across the sequence axis.
options.rationale: Standard Transformer layer normalization computes statistics over the features of each token representation, not across other token positions.

questions.stem: A profiler runs the same full self-attention layer in forward-only inference on sequences of length L and 2L, with batch size, head count, width, and weights fixed. It materializes a score tensor shaped [batch, heads, length, length]. Which finding is consistent?

options.text: The score tensor has about twice as many elements because full attention work scales linearly with token count.
options.rationale: Both sequence axes double, so the number of pairwise score elements grows by about four rather than two.

options.text: The learned query, key, and value parameter tensors occupy about four times the storage because they are indexed by token pairs.
options.rationale: Projection parameters are shared across positions and retain the same shapes when the input sequence length changes.

options.text: The forward score tensor grows about twofold because quadratic attention appears when gradient tensors are retained for training.
options.rationale: The L-by-L score tensor belongs to the forward computation; disabling gradient storage does not remove its pairwise dimensions.

options.text: The score tensor has about four times as many elements, while the learned projection parameter tensors keep the same shapes.
options.rationale: Doubling both length dimensions quadruples the materialized pairwise scores, while shared feature projections remain length independent.

questions.stem: In deterministic evaluation, a token prefix is run once by itself and once with an arbitrary suffix appended. There is no cross-example state. Which hidden-state behavior distinguishes causal self-attention from unrestricted self-attention?

options.text: Earlier states can change in both models because Transformer blocks are bidirectional despite the configured attention mask.
options.rationale: The causal mask removes attention paths from earlier positions to an appended suffix, so architecture name alone does not fix directionality.

options.text: Earlier causal states need remain unchanged during generation; teacher-forced evaluation may expose the appended suffix without violating causality.
options.rationale: The causal visibility rule applies during teacher-forced training and evaluation as well as incremental generation.

options.text: Earlier causal states remain unchanged when the suffix is appended, whereas unrestricted attention may let those states depend on suffix tokens.
options.rationale: Causal masking blocks all paths from a prefix position to later keys; unrestricted attention permits such paths and can change the prefix representation.

options.text: The comparison requires causal prefix positions to be evaluated one at a time, because a parallel masked pass fails to enforce the dependency restriction.
options.rationale: A triangular mask enforces visibility while positions are evaluated in parallel, so the two runs can be compared directly.

questions.stem: A serving optimization reorders the rows of token matrix X with permutation P before a positionless, unmasked self-attention layer H. Downstream code expects outputs in the original token order. Which postprocessing is correct?

options.text: Apply P-transpose to H(PX), since H(PX) = P H(X) and the inverse permutation restores the original row order.
options.rationale: Positionless self-attention is permutation equivariant, so its output rows follow P and can be restored with P-transpose.

options.text: Use H(PX) directly as original-order output, since equivariance keeps the numeric output array fixed when input rows move.
options.rationale: Equivariance moves output rows with input rows; treating the output as fixed confuses equivariance with pointwise invariance.

options.text: Permute the value rows back inside H but leave query-key score rows and columns in their reordered coordinates.
options.rationale: Queries, keys, and values all follow the token-row permutation, so correcting just the values misaligns the attention coordinates.

options.text: Retrain H after introducing P, since shared projection matrices acquire row-specific parameters under the new token ordering.
options.rationale: The same projections are applied at every token row; a row permutation does not alter or reindex their learned parameters.

questions.stem: A classifier applies positionless, unmasked self-attention H and then sums its output rows: r(X) = sum_i H(X)_i. For a permutation P of the token rows, what relation should hold before the final classifier?

options.text: r(PX) may encode P because content-based attention weights reveal the absolute row index even without a positional signal.
options.rationale: Content interactions alone do not attach an absolute index to a row when projections and masks are position independent.

options.text: r(PX) = r(X); self-attention permutes its output rows, and the symmetric sum removes that row permutation.
options.rationale: H(PX) = P H(X), and summing all rows gives the same pooled vector after a permutation.

options.text: r(PX) generally differs because sharing projection weights across rows destroys the permutation relation between H(PX) and H(X).
options.rationale: Applying the same projections to each row is part of why the positionless layer remains permutation equivariant.

options.text: r(PX) generally differs because sum pooling reconstructs the ordering discarded by the equivariant token representations.
options.rationale: A symmetric sum discards row order; it cannot reconstruct an ordering absent from its input representation.

questions.stem: For one attention query, y = sum_i alpha_i v_i and all alpha_i are fixed and positive. A perturbation delta is added to one non-maximum-weight value v_j while queries and keys stay fixed. What is the resulting change before output projection?

options.text: The alpha values stay fixed and y changes by alpha_j times delta, so a non-maximum value still contributes.
options.rationale: With fixed attention weights, linearity of the weighted sum gives y-prime minus y = alpha_j delta.

options.text: The alpha values are recomputed from delta because values participate in the compatibility scores that softmax normalizes.
options.rationale: Queries and keys determine the compatibility scores; perturbing a value leaves those scores and their softmax unchanged.

options.text: The output stays fixed because the key vectors, rather than the value vectors, are combined after the softmax.
options.rationale: The softmax weights multiply the values; keys serve in the score calculation rather than as the output payload.

options.text: The output stays fixed because v_j lacks the largest alpha and softmax attention discards non-maximum positions.
options.rationale: Softmax gives a weighted sum, not an argmax lookup, so a positive non-maximum weight transmits the perturbation.

questions.stem: A multi-query decoder layer has finished processing prefix token t and emitted its attention output. Before token t+1 is processed, which state transition preserves exact access to the prefix while avoiding unnecessary cached tensors?

options.text: Append token t's queries, keys, and values to the cache because the next token reuses all three projected histories.
options.rationale: The next token forms new queries; prior keys and values are the projected histories reused by its attention calculation.

options.text: Append token t's shared key and value to their prefix caches, discard its queries, and form fresh query heads for token t+1.
options.rationale: Exact incremental self-attention retains each prior key-value entry while queries are local to the step that consumes them.

options.text: Replace the prefix cache with token t's key and value because sharing a key-value head also merges the sequence history.
options.rationale: Multi-query sharing reduces the head axis, not the time axis; older prefix entries remain necessary for exact attention.

options.text: Append separate keys and values for all query heads but retain one shared query, because multi-query attention shares the query side.
options.rationale: Multi-query attention keeps multiple query heads and shares the keys and values consumed by those heads.

questions.stem: In a scalar residual diagnostic, R_S(z) = z + S(z), A(z) = 2, and F(z) = ReLU(z). Starting at z = -1, what are R_F(R_A(z)) and R_A(R_F(z)), respectively?

options.text: They are 2 and 1; applying A first changes the input seen by ReLU from a negative value to a positive one.
options.rationale: A first gives R_A(-1) = 1 and then R_F(1) = 2; F first leaves -1, then R_A(-1) = 1.

options.text: They are both 1 because residual paths make the two sublayer orders equivalent despite the ReLU boundary.
options.rationale: The first order moves the intermediate across the ReLU boundary, while the reverse order evaluates ReLU at -1.

options.text: They are both -1 because the identity bypass erases the constant attention branch and the ReLU branch.
options.rationale: The identity is added to each branch output; it does not discard the constant update from A.

options.text: They are both 2 because the two residual maps preserve scalar shape and therefore commute.
options.rationale: Sharing an input-output shape does not make transformations commute; the reverse composition evaluates to 1.

questions.stem: A controlled block test supplies residual vector x and branch vector s independently. It adds the same scalar c to every feature of x while holding s fixed. With unit-scale, zero-bias LayerNorm, how do y = LayerNorm(x + s) and y-prime = x + LayerNorm(s) respond?

options.text: Both stay fixed because layer normalization commutes with moving residual addition across the normalization boundary.
options.rationale: The common shift is normalized away when it is inside LayerNorm, but it remains visible when x is added outside.

options.text: Both shift by c because frozen layer normalization is inactive during inference and leaves its input untouched.
options.rationale: Frozen scale and bias do not disable the feature-wise centering and scaling performed during inference.

options.text: The response depends on the residual vectors at neighboring tokens because layer normalization pools statistics across token positions.
options.rationale: Transformer layer normalization uses the features within the current token representation, not neighboring token rows.

options.text: y stays fixed because the common feature shift is centered away, while y-prime shifts by c through its outside residual path.
options.rationale: LayerNorm(x + c1 + s) equals LayerNorm(x + s), while (x + c1) + LayerNorm(s) equals y-prime + c1.

questions.stem: Using the same learned projections, one inference implementation computes full attention over L positions and another lets each query score at most w nearby keys, with fixed w and without materializing blocked pairs. As L grows, which comparison is correct?

options.text: Full pairwise scoring is O(L squared), restricted scoring is O(Lw), and the shared projection parameter shapes stay fixed.
options.rationale: Full attention scores all position pairs, while a fixed-width neighborhood bounds scores per query without changing the learned feature projections.

options.text: Both scoring patterns are O(L) because full attention processes each token once and has no pairwise length factor.
options.rationale: Full attention forms query-key interactions across L by L position pairs, even though projections are shared by token.

options.text: The restricted model has O(Lw) learned projection parameters because each visible query-key pair needs its own weights.
options.rationale: The projection weights are reused across positions; L and w determine activation work rather than a new parameter set.

options.text: Both are O(L) at inference because quadratic pairwise computation arises from retaining gradients during training.
options.rationale: Gradient storage is separate from forward pairwise scoring; full inference still evaluates quadratically many position pairs.

questions.stem: A teacher-forced decoder evaluates all positions in parallel. A loss reads the hidden state at position i. Through a stack of causal self-attention layers, what gradient path exists to the input activation at a later position j greater than i? Ignore shared-parameter effects.

options.text: A nonzero path exists because Transformer layers are inherently bidirectional even when their attention edges are masked.
options.rationale: Causal masks remove later-to-earlier activation paths; the architecture name does not override those masked edges.

options.text: No such activation path exists; each causal layer blocks later keys from position i, and parallel evaluation does not restore the edge.
options.rationale: The causal dependency graph is preserved under layer composition, so the position-i state is independent of later input activations.

options.text: A nonzero path exists in teacher-forced evaluation because causal masks are applied during generation rather than training.
options.rationale: Teacher-forced causal training applies the same visibility restriction to prevent later-token leakage into earlier predictions.

options.text: The gradient vanishes after serial evaluation, but a parallel masked pass creates a path from later positions to i.
options.rationale: Parallel matrix evaluation respects the mask; scheduling all positions together does not add forbidden graph edges.

questions.stem: Training example A occupies packed decoder positions 0 and 1, and unrelated example B occupies positions 2 and 3. A global lower-triangular mask is used. What extra rule keeps B independent of A?

questions.stem: A query-key dot product sums 16 independent zero-mean coordinate products, each with variance 1. What are the unscaled variance and the variance after division by sqrt(16)?

options.text: Both variances are 1 because dot-product scale is independent of the number of coordinates.

questions.stem: A dot product sums 100 independent zero-mean coordinate products, each with variance 4. What variance remains after standard division by sqrt(100)?

options.rationale: Greater unscaled variance tends toward sharper extremes rather than uniformity and does not establish unit scaled-logit variance.

questions.stem: Assume independent coordinate products with fixed positive per-coordinate variance as key dimension grows. For one realized row, raw logits [3,1,-2] are divided by the positive scale 2 before softmax. Which statement follows?

options.text: Unscaled variance growth motivates the divisor, but the positive scale can put -2 above 3 and reverse the key order.

options.rationale: Growing raw-logit variance tends toward sharper extremes rather than equality, and these stated logits remain distinct after scaling.

questions.stem: Assume independent coordinate products with fixed positive per-coordinate variance as key dimension grows. The same nonconstant realized logit vector is divided by scale 1 in run A and scale 4 in run B before softmax. What comparison follows?

questions.stem: Assume independent coordinate products with fixed positive per-coordinate variance as key dimension grows. For one realized two-key row, raw logits [6,0] are divided by 3 before softmax. Which statement correctly combines the dimension effect with this row?

questions.stem: Head A has key dimension 16 and head B has key dimension 64. In each head, the coordinate products are independent, zero mean, and have variance 1. What are the raw dot-product variances and the variances after division by the square root of each head's dimension?

options.text: The raw variances are 16 and 64, and the two scaled variances are 1 because each divisor's square equals its dimension.

Let p be the first key's softmax probability, and measure local sensitivity to its input logit by p(1-p). Which comparison follows?

questions.stem: A kernel sums d_k independent zero-mean coordinate products of variance 1, with d_k greater than 1, but divides each raw attention logit by d_k instead of sqrt(d_k). Which audit is correct?

options.text: The raw variance is 1 and the output variance is 1/d_k squared, while the common divisor preserves the key order.

questions.stem: A multi-query decoder layer has completed a P-position prompt prefill, then receives one newly generated token to extend the sequence. It has h query heads, one key head, and one value head. Which state transition supports exact incremental self-attention?

options.text: Retain the prompt's Q, K, and V histories, then append the new token's projections because later tokens reuse each projected history.

options.text: F changes by alpha_j times delta while W is unchanged, providing a direct counterexample to functional equivalence at this step.
options.rationale: Fixed weights route the retained value perturbation into F, while W has no row j through which that perturbation can act.

options.text: W matches F after caching position j's past query, because that query reconstructs the evicted value contribution alpha_j times delta.
