questions.stem: At one decoder step, both implementations process a visible prefix of length t. The uncached implementation recomputes that prefix; the exact cached implementation retains t-1 positions, projects the current token, and attends its new query to the t positions. Width and head count are fixed. Which work account is correct?

options.text: Uncached and cached score work are both O(t); caching changes prefix projection work from O(t) to O(1) but full attention is already linear.
options.rationale: The uncached prefix forms a t-by-t score matrix, whereas the cached call forms one growing score row.

options.text: Uncached projection and score work are O(t) and O(t squared); cached projection and score work are O(1) and O(t), respectively.
options.rationale: The cache reuses prior K/V projections but the new query still scores the growing retained prefix.

options.text: Cached score work is O(t), but its t retained K/V rows become learned parameters, so the model's parameter count grows with the prefix.
options.rationale: The cache rows are input-dependent activations; learned projection parameter shapes stay fixed as the prefix grows.

options.text: Uncached and cached score work are both O(t) at inference; the t-squared forward matrix is attributed to gradient-retaining training runs.
options.rationale: Removing backward storage does not remove the uncached forward matrix of pairwise prefix scores.

provenance.source_scope: Vaswani et al. grounds the full score matrix, and Shazeer grounds reuse of past K/V with one new query during incremental inference. The one-step asymptotic partition is original synthesis.

questions.stem: Four decoder calls have visible prefix lengths 1, 2, 3, and 4. Ignore projection and width costs. An uncached call recomputes the full prefix score matrix; an exact cached call forms one new score row. Which total score count and cache classification are correct?

options.text: Both implementations form 10 scores because full attention scores one linear row per prefix length, just as the cached call does.
options.rationale: The uncached calls form square matrices, so their counts are 1, 4, 9, and 16 rather than 1, 2, 3, and 4.

options.text: The totals are 30 uncached and 10 cached, but the 10 retained K/V position entries become learned parameters during generation.
options.rationale: The score totals are right, but cached entries are per-input activations rather than learned model weights.

options.text: The totals are 30 uncached and 10 cached: square-prefix counts sum to 30, row lengths sum to 10, and K/V are activations.
options.rationale: The uncached total is 1 squared plus 2 squared plus 3 squared plus 4 squared, while the cached total is 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4.

options.text: Both implementations form 4 scores because inference removes pairwise forward scoring and leaves one scalar attention result per decoder call.
options.rationale: Inference still computes query-key scores; it omits backward storage, not the forward attention interactions.

provenance.source_scope: Vaswani et al. grounds pairwise score matrices, and Shazeer grounds one-query incremental K/V reuse. The four-call arithmetic and activation-versus-parameter audit are original synthesis.

questions.stem: A frozen encoder-decoder model uses multi-query cross-attention with source length S, h decoder query heads, one encoder-derived key head, one encoder-derived value head, and head width d. The encoded source is unchanged across target steps. Using [sequence, heads, width] and omitting batch, which incremental state account is correct?

options.text: Cache each past target Q beside the encoder K/V and reuse those queries at later target steps instead of forming a fresh Q.
options.rationale: Each target step supplies a new decoder query; past target queries are not the reusable source memory.

options.text: Reuse encoder K/V as [S,h,d] and form Q as [1,1,d], because multi-query cross-attention shares decoder queries rather than encoder keys and values.
options.rationale: Multi-query attention retains h query heads while sharing one encoder-derived K head and one V head.

options.text: Reuse encoder K/V as [1,1,d] because sharing their head axis also collapses the S encoded source positions into one persistent entry.
options.rationale: Head sharing preserves the source sequence axis, so all S encoded positions remain available to each target query.

options.text: Reuse encoder K/V as [S,1,d] across target steps and form each fresh Q as [1,h,d]; decoder self-attention handles growing target history.
options.rationale: The source memory is fixed across target steps, while decoder queries change; target-position growth belongs to decoder self-attention cache, not encoder-derived cross-attention K/V.

provenance.source_scope: Vaswani et al. defines decoder queries over encoder-derived K/V, and Shazeer applies MQA to encoder-decoder attention with shared K/V heads. The cache-reuse comparison across target steps is original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This is dependent transfer within f_transformer_multiquery_state_transition: it contrasts reusable K/V with fresh Q across target steps, while static encoder memory replaces that family's growing decoder self-attention state. It also overlaps f_transformer_cross_attention_direction by assigning decoder Q versus encoder K/V and overlaps f_transformer_multiquery_cache_inventory and f_transformer_multiquery_cache_axes by requiring [S,1,d] K/V and [1,h,d] Q. Those overlaps make the transfer useful practice but not independent-family evidence.
